title: Jobs of Bygone Eras
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss jobs that have disappeared, starting with a Bureau of Labor Statistics-style list of endangered jobs (word processors, typists, door-to-door sales, mail carriers) and John Maynard Keynes's essay on a future without work. They then cover extinct jobs: chariot racers in ancient Rome (Circus Maximus, the racing factions, and the wealthy racer Gaius Diocles), armorers who built plate armor until muskets made it obsolete, court jesters and their satirical role (including Dickie Pierce's death), crossing sweepers in Victorian London, lamplighters who lit gas street lamps, ice cutters who harvested winter ice for icehouses and iceboxes, pin setters who reset bowling pins before automatic pin spotters, and party line telephone operators in rural areas. The episode closes with a listener mail follow-up about Christiania in Copenhagen.

segments.title: Opening banter and extinct jobs preview
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about a Denver live show and preview the episode. They discuss a list of jobs expected to disappear (word processors, typists, door-to-door sales, mail carriers) and Keynes's essay on automation and a future without work.

segments.title: Chariot racing in ancient Rome
segments.summary: Chariot racing is described as an extinct sport, with Circus Maximus, the red, white, blue, green, purple and gold factions, and fan devotion. Racers wore reins tied to their waists and carried knives. The wealthy racer Gaius Diocles, who raced for about 24 years, is discussed, along with the unreliable wealth conversion figure.

segments.title: Armorers and plate armor
segments.summary: Medieval armorers made custom plate armor, passed down father to son, with secrets closely guarded. Steel was costly and reused, so most surviving armor dates to the sixteenth century. Armorers declined as muskets could pierce steel. Civil War soldiers sometimes wore breastplates.

segments.title: Court jesters
segments.summary: The hosts discuss court jesters as educated satirists who could criticize the king, plus other fool types including innocent fools and French fool societies. Jesters sometimes had other duties and fought at the front. Henry II reportedly gave a jester thirty acres. Dickie Pierce, the last known jester, died in 1570 after falling from a pulpit.

segments.title: Crossing sweepers in Victorian London
segments.summary: Crossing sweepers cleared horse manure and filth from street crossings so upper-class pedestrians could avoid it. Often children or disabled people did the work as a last-chance job, with low barriers to entry. The role faded as sanitation improved.

segments.title: Lamplighters
segments.summary: Lamplighters lit and maintained gas street lamps at dusk and extinguished them at dawn, using long poles. A lamplighter covered about 70 to 80 lamps. Some women worked the job. Some English towns still light lamps today.

segments.title: Ice cutting and the icebox
segments.summary: Winter ice was harvested from ponds and rivers using horse-drawn plows and saws, cut into blocks, and stored in sawdust-packed icehouses for summer delivery to iceboxes. Horses that fell through ice were a hazard. The job lasted into the 1930s until refrigeration arrived.

segments.title: Pin setters
segments.summary: Pin boys reset bowling pins by hand for about ten cents a game before automatic pin spotters arrived, invented by Gottfried Schmidt and debuted at the American Bowling Congress tournament. Pin setters faced thrown balls and rowdy bowlers.

segments.title: Party line telephones and rubbering
segments.summary: Rural party lines shared one phone line among many houses, each with a distinct ring. Operators at central handled calls and emergencies signaled with long rings. Neighbors eavesdropping was called rubbering. Pillow Talk is mentioned as a party line film.

segments.title: Listener mail: Christiania follow-up
segments.summary: A listener from Ireland describes visiting Christiania in Copenhagen, noting its rules against running and photography, the illegal cannabis sales, and a favorite restaurant meal.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners, invite emails, and point to additional extinct jobs content on the website.
